chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: Out on the road with Jelly Roll in Pennsylvania coal country
summary: The Morton band played dance halls for mostly white audiences; Procope recalls prejudice in Scranton and that no jazz bands then played concerts. The tour fell apart after a couple of weeks.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: 1929. We just finished with Jelly Roll, right? So you went out on the road with Jelly Roll.

Yes, we left Rose Danceland, and Jelly Roll, of course he had that idea about traveling, you know. That was the big time thing to do. But he had a name even then, you know. He was pretty -- so he took us out of Rose Danceland and we went down in Pennsylvania to the coal regions. That was good dance territory in those days, and we played -- I guess we stayed down there, oh, a couple of weeks I guess. And then it all fell apart. I came back home and -- where did I go then? Oh, I got another job with the dancing schools. The Venetian Gardens down on 58th Street and 8th Avenue, off of -- off of Columbus Circle.
Before you get into that, when you were out in coal regions with Jelly Roll, you played dance halls?
Was it for black people or white people or what?
Well at that time in that part of the

country everybody wasn't that -- I mean it wasn't segregated, you know, in Pennsylvania in those towns. Some were and some wasn't, but it was predominantly white, because there weren't that many black people who lived in that section in the coal regions in Pennsylvania at that time. I remember Scranton, which was -- Scranton, Pennsylvania was about the biggest town in that area. They were quite prejudiced in that town. Because I remember one day the band stopped and we went into a -- I can't remember whether -- I think this was Fletcher Henderson's band, I believe, and we went into this restaurant, and we, you know, sat down and we ordered our food and there was this fellow sitting on the corner and he called the waiter and he resented us being in there. So the waiter said to him -- I remember distinctly, he says, "What are you squawking about? They're ordering steaks. You're eating a hamburger." That's what he told him. You know, just a side joke, you know.
But that's the way it was. It was predominantly, you know, a white audience, white audiences.
Oh, yes, yes. They came to dance, yeah.

At that time this thing about giving jazz concerts, that wasn't the thing. Every time you came to a small town like that it was a dance hall where you played. In fact jazz concerts weren't then. No jazz bands played concerts.
But did the band play hits of the

Oh, no, no, of course not, no. Like the band played about -- I don't know just how many. Maybe 15 Jellyroll Morton tunes, you know. But as I remember he had an audience even then because they'd come up and request things that they had heard on records by Jellyroll, you know. And he didn't have Simon then. Simon didn't go on the trip. I think he went back home to Chicago. And of course I didn't know all of them, you know, because Simon used to play them. I did the best I could with the clarinet work. So that came to an end when we went back to New York. And like I said, he was rehearsing this band to go into Roseland but it never got off the ground. Yeah.
